lessons.title: Planning: vision, analysis and the farm plan
lessons.html:
Levels of planning

Planning at N5 level moves beyond single decisions to structured planning for the whole farm.

  • Strategic planning – long term (3 to 10 years): what kind of farm business do we want to be? Which enterprises, markets and scale?
  • Tactical planning – medium term (1 to 3 years): enterprise mix, investment programme, staffing.
  • Operational planning – short term (season, month, week): planting programmes, grazing plans, work schedules.

Vision and mission

A vision describes where the business wants to be; a mission describes what it does and for whom. Example: To be a profitable, family-owned mixed farm that improves its veld and soils and supplies quality weaners and grain to local buyers. Objectives then make the mission measurable.

SWOT analysis

InternalExternal
Strengths: good soils, reliable borehole, experienced foremanOpportunities: new feedlot buyer nearby, demand for grass-fed beef
Weaknesses: old machinery, high overdraft, poor recordsThreats: drought cycles, input cost increases, stock theft

Strategies are built by using strengths to take up opportunities, fixing weaknesses that block progress and reducing exposure to threats.

The farm plan

The farm plan brings together:

  1. A resource inventory: land use classes, soils, water rights, veld condition, infrastructure, labour, capital.
  2. Enterprise choices supported by gross margins and market analysis.
  3. Physical plans: crop rotation, grazing and fodder flow, stocking rates within the carrying capacity of the veld.
  4. Financial plans: whole-farm and cash flow budgets, investment plans and financing.
  5. An implementation schedule and responsibilities.

Conservation obligations, such as those under the Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983, must be built into the plan.

lessons.title: Organising and delegating
lessons.html:
Organising the farm business

Organising translates plans into a structure of roles, responsibilities and resources. A good structure makes clear who does what, who reports to whom and who has authority to decide.

Organisational structures

  • Simple (line) structure – owner manages directly; suits small farms. Fast decisions but heavy reliance on one person.
  • Functional structure – sections by function, such as production, workshop, finance and administration.
  • Enterprise (divisional) structure – sections by enterprise, such as dairy, crops and packhouse, each with its own manager responsible for results.

Draw an organogram and supplement it with job descriptions so each role's duties, authority and reporting line are written down.

Principles of organising

  • Unity of command – each worker reports to one supervisor.
  • Span of control – the number of people one supervisor can manage effectively. It depends on the complexity and spread of the work; a supervisor of a picking team in one block can manage more people than one overseeing tasks across distant camps.
  • Authority matched to responsibility – people held responsible for results must have the authority and resources to achieve them.

Delegation

Delegation means giving a subordinate the authority to carry out a task while the manager remains accountable. Effective delegation frees the manager for planning and develops staff.

  1. Choose the task and the right person.
  2. Explain the result expected, the standard and the deadline.
  3. Give the necessary authority and resources, and tell others about it.
  4. Agree on check-in points.
  5. Monitor without taking over, and give feedback.

Common reasons managers fail to delegate include lack of trust, fear of mistakes and the belief that it is quicker to do it oneself. Over time, failing to delegate limits the growth of the business.

Coordination

Regular short meetings, a shared work calendar and clear communication channels keep sections aligned, for example making sure the workshop has the sprayer ready when the crop manager needs it.

Key points

  • Plan at strategic, tactical and operational levels.
  • Use vision, mission and SWOT analysis to build strategy.
  • A farm plan integrates resources, enterprises, physical and financial plans.
  • Organise with clear structures, job descriptions and sensible spans of control.
  • Delegate authority with clear expectations; the manager stays accountable.
